The question in this verse is put to the people who had made things unlawful on their own authority. "Ask, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Who has forbidden the adornments and lawful provisions Allah has brought forth for His servants?” Say, “They are for the enjoyment of the believers in this worldly life, but they will be exclusively theirs on the Day of Judgment. This is how We make Our revelations clear for people of knowledge.”" The verse refutes anyone who forbids a kind of food, drink or clothing according to his own understanding, without resting on what Allah has legislated.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Ask, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Who has forbidden the adornments ... Allah has brought forth for His servants?”"** is a rebuke in the form of a question, and the answer is meant to be obvious. The adornments meant are the clothes they had declared off limits for the days of the ḥajj, whether in the sacred precinct or during the ṭawāf of the Kaʿbah. The clothing named is the adornment that Allah created for His servants.

**"and lawful provisions"** translates aṭ-Ṭayyibāt, the good and pure things of sustenance. It names meat and fat, because in the days of ignorance people used to deprive themselves of meat and fat during the days of pilgrimage. The whole question is about ḥalāl, what Allah has made lawful, set against the ḥarām they were treating as though it were lawful.

**"Say, “They are for the enjoyment of the believers in this worldly life"** is the first half of the answer. In this world the good things are shared out among everyone. The believers have the right to them, and other people come to enjoy them alongside them.

**"but they will be exclusively theirs on the Day of Judgment"** is the second half, and it is the part that matters. On the Day of Resurrection these things will be for the believers and for nobody else, since the disbelievers will have no share in them and have been kept out of Paradise. What the phrase says is that the good things of this world belong by right to the obedient servants of Allah, and that in the life to come they will be theirs alone.

**"This is how We make Our revelations clear for people of knowledge."** is the close. The verses are set out in detail for people who reflect, because they are the ones who profit from them.

### Three ways of reading the promise

The sentence about the believers has been explained in more than one way, and the explanations sit together.

On the first, all the blessings and comforts of this world are the rightful share of the obedient believers, with the safeguard that they must not become a cause of trouble for them in the Hereafter. That was the explanation given by ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbās. The disbelievers and the sinners receive these blessings too, and often they receive more of them, but what they receive becomes their ruin in the Hereafter and brings on a punishment that lasts for ever. Once the outcome is put beside the enjoyment, this is not the kind of comfort and honour anyone would welcome.

On the second, every blessing and comfort of this world is laced with unending effort, with the fear that it may decline, and with anxiety that never stops. Pure blessing and pure comfort simply do not exist here. Whoever receives these blessings on the Day of Judgment will receive them in a state of absolute purity, with no effort to reach them, no fear that they will decline or be lost, and no worry after them.

On the third, the arrangement of this world is what it is because this world is the place of deeds and not the place of reward. No line can be drawn here between the genuine and the counterfeit, or between the good and the bad, in the matter of what is available. The table is open to everyone, and the blessings come from ar-Raḥmān, the All-Merciful, who is the Most Compassionate to the whole world. But the arrangements in this world follow the will of Allah, and it is His established practice that when the obedient believers fall short in their duties, other people overcome them and take the treasures of worldly blessing. The believing servants are then left with hunger and poverty. This law works only here, in the place of deeds. Once the Hereafter comes, all blessings and all comfort are kept back for the obedient.

### Why forbidding good things is not religion

The people who have been reprimanded in this verse are the ones who go to excess in worship and bring self-invented restrictions into it. They hold back from what Allah has made lawful and make it unlawful for themselves, and then they call that act obedience to Allah and worship of Him. That is what the disbelievers of Makkah did. They thought it was not permissible to wear clothes during the circuit in the days of the ḥajj, and they thought that holding back from good food that Allah had made lawful was an act of worship.

Setting something as lawful or unlawful is the sole right of the One who created it. Nobody else is permitted to interfere in the matter. So the people who treat good clothing and good food made lawful by Allah as forbidden to themselves deserve His anger and His punishment. Living in tattered rags when a person has the means is not a teaching of Islam, and it is not something worth imitating, as some ignorant people suppose.

Many of the righteous elders of the early period and the jurists among the Imāms of Islam, whom Allah had given good means, used to wear elegant and even expensive clothes. The Prophet ﷺ himself, when his means allowed it, adorned his body with the best of clothing. One narration says that when he came out one day he was wearing a cloak worth a thousand dirhams. Abū Ḥanīfah is reported to have used a cloak worth four hundred guineas. Mālik always used decent and elegant clothing, and someone had taken it on himself to supply him with three hundred and sixty pairs of clothes each year. A pair that he wore for a day he would not wear again, because after a single day he gave it away to a poor student.

The reason for all of it is a saying of the Holy Prophet ﷺ. When the Exalted Lord blesses a servant of His with ample means, He likes to see the effect of that blessing on the things around him, and his clothing is one of them. Letting such a blessing be seen is therefore a form of gratitude. The opposite attitude, wearing worn-out or untidy clothes when a person has the means, is ingratitude, and the Sunnah asks for neither extreme.

Two things must be guarded against at the same time: hypocrisy and showing off, and pride and arrogance. A person should not dress well in order to put himself above others or to establish that he is superior or special. And the righteous elders of the early period were free of any such thing.

### Why the same people wore plain clothes

The Prophet ﷺ, ʿUmar and some of the Companions are reported to have worn ordinary or patched clothing, and there were two reasons for it.

The first is that whatever came into their hands they spent on the poor and the needy and on their religious aims. For their own persons there was too little left to afford fine clothes. The second is that they were the leaders of the people, and they kept themselves in that plain and inexpensive bearing so that others with ample means would take the lesson, and so that the ordinary people and the poor would not be overawed by their wealth.

The same holds for the noble Sufis. When they keep those who are new to the path from fine clothing and good food, they do not mean that giving these things up for good is a work of merit. Far from it. What they are doing is putting a brake on the desires of the self during the first stage of the search for truth, and the brake is a treatment and a medicine. When the seeker reaches the stage where he has learned to control his desires, and the self can no longer be caught by what is unlawful, then all the masters of the spiritual orders use good clothing and good food and recommend them, exactly as the early righteous elders did. At that point these fine blessings become a way of recognising the Creator and drawing near to Him.

### The way of the Prophet ﷺ in food and clothing

The essential practice of the Holy Prophet ﷺ, the Companions and those who followed them is that a person should not be unnaturally concerned about food and clothing. What is within easy reach is good enough, and it should be used with gratitude. Suppose the clothing is coarse and the food plain. There is no need then to bother about finding something finer by borrowing, or to fret so much over what is missing that a person falls into some other difficulty.

And the opposite is equally true. When fine clothing and good food are available without effort, there is no need to go to the other extreme and ruin them or refuse to use them at all. Going out of one's way after fine clothes and fine food is one constraint a person puts on himself. Doing the reverse, wasting what is good and choosing what is worse, is another self-imposed constraint, and a blameworthy one.

### The inner reading

The tongue has an ornament, and it is dhikr, the remembrance of Allah. The heart has an ornament, and it is reflection. There is nothing that has no ornament. For the soul, the ornament is beautiful practice joined to the quality of struggle. The ornament of the heart is unbroken union at the moment of contemplation. The ornament of the secret core is the realities of nearness in the field of face to face vision.

The question in the verse, about who has forbidden the adornment of God, points to the fact that these adornments are not held back from the seekers, and are not refused to the hearts that are present. The storehouse is full, and all it waits for is the seeker. The table of gentleness and mercy is spread, and all it waits for is the eater. One of the masters of the path said in whispered prayer:

> O seekers, hurry, for the hard cash is near. O night travellers, do not sleep, for the morning is near. O hurriers, be glad, for the abode is near. O thirsty ones, be patient, for the spring is near. O strangers, rejoice, for the master of hospitality is near. O seekers of the Friend, be glad, for the answer is near. O Opener of my heart, what harm would it do You to open my heart and lay Your balm on my spirit? How can I look for gain when my hands hold no capital? What if You threw me into good fortune out of Your bounty?

### In short

- The question is a rebuke to those who made things unlawful on their own authority, without resting on what Allah legislated.
- The adornments and the good provisions named were the clothing forbidden during the pilgrimage and the meat and fat forbidden during it.
- The good things of this world are open to everyone, and on the Day of Judgment they are for the believers exclusively. Reading the promise three ways, they are the believers' rightful share now, they will be pure of every effort and fear then, and this world is the place of deeds rather than of reward.
- Wearing good clothing when a person has the means is a form of gratitude, since Allah likes to see the effect of His blessing on His servant. Worn-out clothing when a person has the means is ingratitude.
- The plain clothing of the Prophet ﷺ and the early generations came from generosity with what they had and from a wish not to overawe the people, and the Sufis only withhold good things from a beginner as a treatment.

33.text:
The verse turns from what was wrongly forbidden to what is truly forbidden. "Say, “My Lord has only forbidden open and secret indecencies, sinfulness, unjust aggression, associating ˹others˺ with Allah ˹in worship˺—a practice He has never authorized—and attributing to Allah what you do not know.”" The list is short and each item is a heading. Together they cover nearly every kind of prohibition there is, whether it belongs to belief or to conduct, and whether it is done by a person alone or takes away the rights of somebody else.

### Phrase by phrase

**"open and secret indecencies"** is the first item. The Arabic word is fāḥishah, and it covers grave sins, of which the plainest is fornication. The open kind is done in the sight of people. The secret kind is hidden and done privately, and it takes in the taking of secret lovers.

**"sinfulness"** is the second. The Arabic word is al-ithm, and it covers every sin that falls on a person himself, the disobedience that concerns him and his own Lord and takes nothing from anybody else. One poet pictured it by saying that he sipped at sin until his mind wandered off, which is what sin does to a mind, and then drank jars of it out in the open.

**"unjust aggression"** is the third, and it covers the sins that concern other people, the wrongs done to their persons, their wealth or their honour. It is the overbearing that takes what is not one's own and puts a weight on those who cannot resist.

**"associating ˹others˺ with Allah ˹in worship˺—a practice He has never authorized"** is the fourth. What is being named is shirk, the greatest of the prohibitions, and the phrase adds what makes it indefensible. No scripture and no proof has ever come down sanctioning it. It is the one ḥarām that no prophet and no book ever left room for, and the verse names it among the ordinary wrongs to show that the prohibition stands on its own evidence. The verse does not argue about which partner is being associated. It points out that nothing at all has been sent to warrant the association.

**"and attributing to Allah what you do not know"** is the fifth, and it is the one that ties this verse back to the two before it. It covers saying things about Allah without knowledge, in His names, in His attributes, in His actions and in His sacred law. It covers forbidding crops and cattle, and it covers forbidding good things and clothing. It is the same charge that was laid against the people who defended the naked circuit of the House with the claim that Allah had commanded it.

### Why this list and these people

This detail was given here because it covers nearly every kind of prohibition and sin, whether the matter belongs to belief or to conduct, whether it was done by a person on his own or took the rights of others. Aḥmad recorded from ʿAbdullah, and the two ṣaḥīḥ collections carry the report, that the Prophet ﷺ named the worst of the major sins, and the list he gave includes the wrongs done to parents and the false word.

It was also given because the people of the age of ignorance were caught up in all of these crimes at once. They had taken partners alongside Allah, they had invented laws about their cattle and their crops, they had wronged one another, and they had done indecent things in the open. So the verse is a further demonstration of their ignorance, and the shape of the ignorance is worth pausing on. They held back from what had been made lawful for them, and at the same time they did not hesitate for a moment to do what had been declared unlawful.

### Two kinds of loss

The hint in the passage is that these people were suffering from a twofold ignorance.

On one side they deprived themselves of the good things of life that Allah had made lawful for them, denying themselves their use as though the things were unlawful, and doing so for no reason at all. On the other side, there were things that were genuinely and really unlawful, things whose use would bring the anger of Allah and punishment in the Hereafter, and those they embraced with both arms. They discovered only afterwards that what they had embraced was their own undoing in the life to come. So they were robbed twice over: robbed of the blessings they had in this world, and robbed of the blessings they had a chance of having in the next.

### The danger of excess in religion

There is a lesson here that goes well beyond the people it was addressed to. It is a necessary outcome of going to excess in religion, and of introducing invented practices into it, that the people who get caught up in it become habitually heedless about the root of the religion and its essential requirements.

So the harm from excess and invention is twofold. Getting involved with them is a sin in itself. And then, set against that, there is something far graver: the loss of the religion of Allah as it truly is, and of the genuine way of the Holy Prophet ﷺ. A person may be so busy with the addition he has made that he no longer notices what he has dropped.

### How the same fault appears in every age

The mistake is not confined to one period. Some of the Arab tribes used to perform their circuit of the Kaʿbah with nothing on at all, thinking that it brought them nearer to God. And in the same period they would hold back from certain things, such as goat's milk or meat, when setting out on the ḥajj, imagining that they were doing something great and righteous. The cattle they had declared off limits in this way are named in Sūrat al-Anʿām, and the answer to the whole practice is the command to turn away from the impurity of idolatry and from the words of falsehood (22:30). As-Suddī and Mujāhid are among those who read the verse in this setting.

Actions of that kind have been taken up by people in every age. Such people do not build the requirements of religion into their ordinary daily life. Then, on certain occasions, they make a display of living by the religion of God while attending to irrelevant and pointless observances, and they claim that these trivialities are what carry out God's will to the fullest extent.

What God wants instead is set out in the verse. A person should hold back from being a spendthrift, which is to say that he should not cross the limits God laid down. He should not treat permitted things as forbidden, or forbidden things as permitted. He should turn away from shameful acts, and from whatever ordinary sense can see to be plainly evil. He should give up all excesses. When the truth appears to him, he should accept it and put everything else aside. He should clean himself thoroughly of ascribing partners to God, and he should not give to anyone the sublime relationship that belongs by right to the one God alone.

And one thing above all should not happen. A person should not choose a path for himself and then lay it on God with no reason for doing so. He should remain a servant of God throughout, and should not take up ways that are unfitting for a servant of God.

### The blessings of the two worlds

The two kinds of blessing are not the same kind. In the Hereafter the good things of God come as a reward, and a reward is given only to those God decides to send to Paradise. The blessings received in this world are different. They come for a limited period, and they come for the purpose of a test, so a person receives a share in them according to the paper he has been set.

The way to meet the requirements of that test is not to keep away from the provisions God has given for it. It is to use them inside the limits set for them. A person should answer the blessing of God with gratitude, and not with renunciation or with a display of bravado.

### In short

- The verse lists five things that are truly forbidden, and the list covers nearly every kind of prohibition there is.
- Open and secret indecencies are the first, sinfulness the second, unjust aggression the third, associating others with Allah the fourth, and saying about Allah what is not known the fifth.
- Sin covers what a person does against his own soul, and unjust aggression covers the wrongs done to others, so the two together take in conduct on both sides.
- The people addressed were caught up in every one of the five at once, and the shape of their ignorance was that they refused what was lawful for them and embraced what was unlawful.
- Excess in religion and invented practices carry a double harm, since the practice itself is a sin and the loss of the religion as it truly is is graver still.

34.text:
The two verses before this one described people who took what was ḥalāl as ḥarām and made what was ḥarām lawful for themselves. This verse states where that ends. "For each community there is an appointed term. When their time arrives, they can neither delay it for a moment, nor could they advance it". A term has been fixed for every people, and the fixed thing cannot be moved in either direction.

### Phrase by phrase

**"For each community"** means every generation and every nation, the whole ummah (community), and every people that has a religion.

**"there is an appointed term"** means a time already set, the time destined for their destruction as a people.

**"When their time arrives, they can neither delay it for a moment"** means that not one fraction of a second of reprieve is given after the appointed hour has come.

**"nor could they advance it"** means the opposite, that the destruction does not come before the appointed hour by so much as a fraction of a second either.

### What the fixity of the term is saying

Those who are committing these excesses are living in the sunshine of the blessings of Allah, and no punishment seems anywhere near them. This verse tells them not to be fooled by that. The practice of Allah is that He grants a long leash to sinners in His mercy, so that they might somehow stop what they are doing. The length of that leash, and the hour at which the respite ends, are fixed in His ultimate knowledge. When the time comes it comes, neither too late nor too soon, and the criminals are taken by the punishment. Sometimes the punishment comes down on them in this world, and if it does not visit them here it waits for them soon after their death.

The wording is worth a note. Naming both the delay and the advance is a way of speaking that makes the point land. It is rather like asking a shopkeeper whether his last price is more or less, where the real question is the lower price and the mention of the higher one is only a subordinate part of the sentence. The real point here is that there will be no delay after the appointed time. Saying "nor advance it" as well brings the matter closer to ordinary understanding.

### What the term is fixed against

For an individual, the plan of creation gives him room to do well or badly in this world until the period of his trial is over. For a community or a nation, the matter works differently. There is no such limit on the enforcement of God's decision, because the decision about a community is taken on the basis of how that community responded once the truth had been brought to it.

The end of a nation's period comes in one of two ways. One of them is a punishment sent down from outside the ordinary course of things, which destroys the people outright. The other is being thrown down from the rank of honour and supremacy they had held. The decision about Heaven or Hell as a person's final destination is taken on the basis of his response once the truth has appeared before him, supported by arguments whose reasonableness his own intellect can confirm. That means the message reaching him in the full sense. And then, if a man still refuses to accept the truth, he does so out of egotism, because the wish to keep his own superiority stops him from lowering himself in front of the truth.

### In short

- Every community has a term already fixed, and when the hour comes it cannot be moved forward or back.
- The respite granted to sinners is long, and the length of it is fixed in the knowledge of Allah, so no one should mistake patience for forgetfulness.
- The punishment may come in this world, and if it does not, it waits on the other side of death.
- A nation is judged by how it answered the truth once the truth had reached it, and the man who refuses after that refuses out of egotism.

35.text:
The address returns to all humankind. "O children of Adam! When messengers from among yourselves come to you reciting My revelations—whoever shuns evil and mends their ways, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve". The verse names what a messenger does, and then names what the answer to him looks like.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O children of Adam!"** is the address to the whole of the human race.

**"When messengers from among yourselves come to you"** carries a point in the words "from among you". The messengers are human beings like the people they are sent to, and not a separate order of being.

**"reciting My revelations"** describes what the messenger does with what he brings. It means setting out the commands and the prohibitions, explaining them as he recites them.

**"whoever shuns evil"** means whoever believes in the Scripture and the messenger. The fear of Allah, and staying away from what has not been allowed, is what the word covers.

**"and mends their ways"** means that he puts right what lies between him and his Lord. It also means making right what he does.

**"there will be no fear for them"** takes away the fear of the torment.

**"nor will they grieve"** takes away the second grief, which is grief over the good things of Paradise they might miss. One gloss words it as grieving about the pleasures that passed them by in this world.

### The two halves of the answer

The verse puts two things together in the answer, and both are needed. One is taqwā, the fear of Allah and the keeping away from what He has not allowed. The other is setting things right. A person who keeps away from forbidden things but leaves his conduct unrepaired has done half of it, and so has the person who repairs his conduct without keeping away.

And what follows is stated positively. The believer is not merely let off. He is told that the fear is gone from him and the sadness too, so that the two things that weigh heaviest on a person are taken away at once.

### In short

- The verse addresses all humankind and says that the messengers come from among the people themselves.
- The answer that saves a person has two halves, keeping away from what is prohibited and putting right what lies between him and his Lord.
- What is promised is the removal of both fears at once, that of the torment and that of missing the good things that were prepared.

36.text:
The other side of the same matter. "But those who receive Our revelations with denial and arrogance will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever".

### Phrase by phrase

**"But those who receive Our revelations with denial"** means those who deny the Scripture and the messenger, and who deny the signs themselves.

**"and arrogance"** names the second fault, and it is a distinct one. Their hearts denied the signs, and then they were too proud to live by them. The word covers scorning them and refusing to believe in them.

**"will be the residents of the Fire"** is the sentence. They are its rightful owners, and the phrase carries the sense that the Fire is what belongs to them as their due.

**"They will be there forever"** means the dwelling has no end to it. There is no dying in it and no being removed from it.

### The two faults together

The verse is worth reading beside the one before it. There, the ones who were saved were saved by two things, keeping away from the forbidden and repairing their conduct. Here, the ones who are lost are lost by two things, denial in the heart and arrogance in the bearing. And the order matters. The denial comes first, and the arrogance is what keeps it in place, because a person who has decided in his heart that a thing is not true still needs something to hold him there.

### In short

- The verse names two faults together, denial of the signs and the arrogance that scorns them.
- The Fire is described as what belongs to such people by right, and the dwelling has no end.
- The two faults stand opposite the two parts of the answer in the verse before it.

37.text:
The scene begins to move. "Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah or deny His revelations? They will receive what is destined for them, until Our messenger-angels arrive to take their souls, asking them, “Where are those ˹false gods˺ you used to invoke besides Allah?” They will cry, “They have failed us,” and they will confess against themselves that they were indeed disbelievers". The verse asks a question whose answer is meant to be nobody, and then it follows the wrongdoer from the provisions of this life to the moment his support is tested.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Who does more wrong"** asks who is more insolent and bolder in the face of Allah.

**"than those who fabricate lies against Allah"** names the first kind of wrongdoer. What he does is invent something about Allah. He gives Him a partner, or finds a defect in Him, or puts into His mouth a statement He never made.

**"or deny His revelations"** names the second kind. What is denied is Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an, and the signs that guide to the right way of life. None of the two is more unjust than the other, because both of them come to the same thing, which is settling the truth by one's own decision.

**"They will receive what is destined for them"** names the share that reaches them from the Preserved Tablet, al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ, and from the Book of decrees. The share is their appointed lot. What is meant is each person's deeds, his allotted provision and his age. Another reading spells it out as what they were promised in the Book, such as their faces being turned black and their eyes blue. Muhammad bin Kaʿb al-Quraẓī said that the phrase refers to the appointed portion for each person. Ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas and ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said the same.

**"until Our messenger-angels arrive to take their souls"** marks the end of the portion. The messengers are the angel of death and his helpers, and they come to gather them and take their souls.

**"asking them, “Where are those ˹false gods˺ you used to invoke besides Allah?”"** is the question the angels put to them. They horrify them with it: where are the partners you used to call on in the world, worshipping them instead of Allah? Call them now, so that they may save you from what you are in.

**"They will cry, “They have failed us”"** is the answer. It means they are lost to us, and there is no benefit or help to be hoped for from them. Another reading has it that they are gone from us and not present before us, so that we cannot see them.

**"and they will confess against themselves that they were indeed disbelievers"** is the last line. They admit it and proclaim it against themselves, and the admission is made at the point where it can no longer help them.

### Two passages about the same people

What the Qur'an says of such people elsewhere is that they will never succeed. Their enjoyment is brief, and then their return is to Allah, and then He will make them taste the severest torment for the disbelief they held to (10:69-70). And again: if a person disbelieves, his disbelief should not grieve you, since the return of all of it is to Allah, and He will tell them what they did, and He knows what is in the breasts of people, and He let them enjoy themselves for a little while (31:23-24).

### The props that people trust

Whenever a person rejects the truth, he does it imagining that he has something behind him. He may be relying on his wealth and his power, or on the respect and the popularity he enjoys. He may feel sure that his personal arrangements are in such good order that refusing the truth will do him no harm at all, and that the whole matter is his own to settle and he has some say in it. He may take pride in a clever tongue, and use it to dress up his own ideas until they sound as though they came straight from God.

All of these are serious misreadings. What he has taken for supports on which he can depend for salvation are the very things that were given to him as his test. Once the Day of Resurrection comes and all these false props walk off and leave him, the lesson will be easy to read. He had been refusing the truth out of plain ignorance, and he had kept quoting principles the whole time to make the refusal look considered.

### In short

- No one is more unjust than the person who invents a lie about Allah or denies what He has revealed.
- Such people receive their appointed share of this world from the Book of decrees, which covers their deeds, their provision and their term.
- The angels come for their souls and put the question that tests the props they leaned on, and the props fail.
- Their confession is made when it can no longer help them, and the Qur'an states elsewhere that their enjoyment is brief and their end is the severest torment.

38.text:
The answer comes from above. "Allah will say, “Enter the Fire along with the ˹evil˺ groups of jinn and humans that preceded you.” Whenever a group enters Hell, it will curse the preceding one until they are all gathered inside, the followers will say about their leaders, “Our Lord! They have misled us, so multiply their torment in the Fire.” He will answer, “It has already been multiplied for all, but you do not know.”" The verse sets out what the people of the Fire do to one another once they are inside it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Enter the Fire along with the ˹evil˺ groups of jinn and humans that preceded you."** is the command given to those who associated others with Allah, invented lies about Him and denied His signs. The groups they enter among are their likes and their similars in conduct, the disbelieving nations that passed away before them, from among jinn and human beings. One reading places the phrase about the Fire directly on the command to enter.

**"Whenever a group enters Hell, it will curse the preceding one"** describes what happens as they arrive. Each community curses its sister community, the one that came in before it, because it was through that one that it went astray.

**"until they are all gathered inside"** means they follow one another in until the first of them and the last of them are together in the Fire.

**"the followers will say about their leaders"** identifies the two parties. The last of them to arrive are the followers, and the first of them are the ones they revered and followed.

**"“Our Lord! They have misled us, so multiply their torment in the Fire.”"** is the request of the followers, and it is a complaint laid before Allah rather than an argument among themselves. Multiply their share of the torment, they say.

**"He will answer, “It has already been multiplied for all, but you do not know.”"** is the answer. The words carry the sense that what they asked for has been done, and that each has been recompensed according to his deeds. The reason they do not know it is the severity of the torment itself.

### What the leaders and the followers were to each other

In the world these two groups behaved towards one another as friends anxious for each other's good, ready to give up something of their own for the other. No wish of the ordinary people went unhonoured by the leaders, and the ordinary people in turn made heroes out of the leaders. When they are trapped in the fire, the artificial veils drop from their eyes and each is seen as he truly is.

Then the conversation runs as follows. The followers turn on the leaders and call down curses on them. What a leadership it was, they say, that showed them one spectacle and then pushed them into this. Their words are the words of people who have just seen what they were shown. The leaders answer that the followers wanted a religion to their own liking, and that finding such a religion with them, they rushed towards them. They add that during that very period there were servants of God calling them towards the path of real success, that their call was heard, and that no attention was paid to it.

The leaders then say to the followers that they are in no way better than they are. Leadership was taken up in pursuit of desire, and the following was done for the sake of desire as well. So both parties stand in the same position, and both are liable for the same punishment that has been laid down for their deeds. On this reading, the word for community means the leaders who misguide, and the word for the sister community means the misguided general public.

The followers then put their request to God, that the leaders misled them and should therefore be given double the punishment. The reply is that the leaders are already receiving a doubled punishment, and that the followers do not know it. The plain fact behind the exchange is that in the fire whatever punishment a person is given feels so severe that he thinks nobody else can be in such agony. Everyone there feels himself the worst afflicted.

So the bond that held the two groups together in the world is reversed. In the world, self-interested leaders and self-interested followers were linked in strong friendship, each group speaking well of the other and each finding words for the other's good. In the Hereafter the one group hates the other, and each tries to push the other towards the worst of fates.

### What the Qur'an says of the two parties elsewhere

The scene is set out in several other places. On the Day when their faces are turned over in the Fire, they will wish they had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger. They will say that they obeyed their chiefs and their great ones, and that those misled them from the right way, and they will ask for a double torment for them (33:66-68). And there is the scene of the followers who see the torment and hear the ones they followed declaring that they have nothing to do with them. At that moment every tie that joined the two parties is severed. Those who followed will wish they had another chance to return, so that they could declare themselves innocent of them as they had declared themselves innocent of them, and Allah will show them their deeds as regrets, and they will never come out of the Fire (2:166-167).

A further passage gives the exchange between the arrogant and those they counted weak. The arrogant will ask whether they held the weak back from guidance after it came to them, and will say that it was the weak who were the criminals. Those who were counted weak will answer that it was the plotting of the arrogant by night and day, when they ordered them to disbelieve in Allah and set up rivals to Him. Then each party will conceal its own regret when it sees the torment, and iron collars will be put round the necks of those who disbelieved, who are recompensed for nothing except what they used to do (34:32-33).

The burdens are described as well. For those who disbelieved and held others back from the path of Allah, the torment is increased (16:88). Their own loads are carried by them, and loads beyond their own as well (29:13), and something also of the weight of those they led astray in ignorance (16:25).

And the example of Ibrāhīm (Abraham), al-Khalīl, is on record for the same truth. He said to his people that on the Day of Resurrection they would deny each other (29:25).

### In short

- The evil groups of jinn and human beings enter the Fire together, and each arriving group curses the group that came before it.
- The followers blame the leaders before Allah and ask for their torment to be multiplied, and the answer is that it has already been multiplied for all.
- The leaders answer that the followers wanted a religion to their own liking, and that both parties stand in the same position.
- In the world the two groups praised each other, and in the Fire each tries to push the other towards the worst of fates.
- Every one of them feels his own punishment to be the worst, and the Qur'an says elsewhere that the ties between them are cut and their regret is concealed.

39.text:
The leaders have the last word in the exchange. "Then the leaders will say to their followers, “You were no better than us! So taste the torment for what you used to commit.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then the leaders will say to their followers"** puts the first party in the place of the speaker. The followed now answer the followers.

**"You were no better than us!"** is the substance of the answer. The followers had asked for a double punishment on the leaders on the ground that they had been led astray, and the answer removes the ground. You did not disbelieve because of us, they say, since you and we stand together in this situation. Another reading of the words is that the followers have no advantage over the leaders that would earn them any lightening of the punishment. And another says simply that they disbelieved just as the leaders disbelieved, and worshipped others beside Allah just as the leaders did.

**"So taste the torment"** is the invitation to share what the leaders are tasting.

**"for what you used to commit"** gives the reason. The punishment is for what they used to earn, for the words and the deeds of idolatry they kept up through their life in this world.

### Why the answer closes the argument

As-Suddī put the sense of the answer in one line: you were led astray as we were led astray. That is the whole of it. The followers had presented themselves as people who were taken off the road by somebody else. The leaders point out that nobody took them anywhere. They went where they wanted to go, and they found leaders who told them what they wanted to hear.

There is no excuse at the end for having followed what was false, because the call of the truth had been there the whole time alongside the call of the leaders, and both were heard. So the followers taste the punishment exactly as the leaders taste it, because each of them earned it.

### In short

- The leaders answer the followers by telling them that the following was their own doing and that they stand in the same situation.
- The words are explained in more than one way, all of them arriving at the same sense, that the followers were led astray exactly as the leaders were.
- There is no excuse at the end for having followed what was false, since the call of the truth had been there to hear.
- Both parties taste the punishment, and each tastes it for what he earned.

40.text:
The passage brings the two groups to their destinations. "Surely those who receive our revelations with denial and arrogance, the gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise until a camel passes through the eye of a needle. This is how We reward the wicked". The verse names an impossibility and uses it to measure another one. A camel cannot go through the eye of a needle, and the people described here cannot enter Paradise.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Surely those who receive our revelations with denial and arrogance"** names the people. They deny the signs and they scorn them, which is to say that they refuse to believe in them and they refuse to be ruled by them.

**"the gates of heaven will not be opened for them"** has been read in two ways, and both readings are carried. Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Ibn ʿAbbās said that their good deeds and their supplication will not rise through those gates. The report reaches that reading through al-ʿAwfī and through ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah, and ath-Thawrī narrated it from Layth, who had it from ʿAṭāʾ, who had it from Ibn ʿAbbās. The second reading is that the gates will not be opened for the souls of the disbelievers, which is what aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, and what as-Suddī and several others said as well. Ibn Jurayj combined the two, saying that the gates will not be opened for their deeds or for their souls. And that combined reading is the strongest, and Allah knows best.

**"nor will they enter Paradise until a camel passes through the eye of a needle"** puts the two impossibilities side by side. The word used is the word for a camel, and Ibn Masʿūd said it means the male of the species. A second narration gives it as the mate of the she camel instead. There is also a variant recitation reported from Ibn ʿAbbās by way of Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah, in which the word is not the word for a camel at all but a word meaning a thick rope, so that the sentence reads: until a thick rope goes through a needle's eye. A rope and a needle, or a camel and a needle, make the same point. The opening the camel would have to pass through is one of the smallest openings there is, and the camel is one of the largest animals. Their entry into Paradise is exactly as possible as that. And since the entry is impossible, what the verse proves is that the punishment of the Fire for these people is never going to end.

**"This is how We reward the wicked"** is the sentence passed at the end of the verse, and the wicked here are the idolaters, the ones who were sinful through disbelief.

### The report of the soul at death

The second reading of the gates is supported by a report from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, which Abū Dāwūd, an-Nasāʾī, Ibn Mājah and Aḥmad all recorded in detail. A summary follows.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ attended the funeral of one of the Anṣār, and while the grave was still being prepared he sat down on an open patch of ground, and the Companions sat around him in silence. He raised his head and spoke of the death of the wicked, and then of the soul of such a person being carried up to the heaven. He said:

> So they carry it up, and it does not pass by a gathering of the angels without one of them asking whose wicked soul this is. They answer with the name of such and such, using the worst of the names he was called by in his life. When they reach the lowest heaven, they ask that its door be opened for the soul, and it is not opened for it.

And then the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse, about the gates of heaven not being opened for them. That portion belongs to a long hadith, and it is not the whole of it.

In the fuller narration the Prophet ﷺ described both journeys side by side. For a believing servant of Allah, angels come down from the heaven with radiant white faces, carrying a shroud and a fragrance from Paradise, and they sit in front of the dying man. Then the angel of death comes and says to the rūḥ, the soul: O soul at peace, come out to the forgiveness and the pleasure of your Lord. The soul comes out of the body as easily as water pours from a skin bag when its mouth is opened, and the angel of death takes it into his hands and hands it to the angels waiting there. Wherever the group meets other angels on the way, the question is asked whose soul this is, and the answer gives the man's name and the title he was known by, as an honour done to him. At the first heaven the gate is opened for him, and more angels join the company until the seventh heaven is reached. Then Allah says that the record of this servant's deeds is to be written in ʿIlliyyīn, and the soul is sent back to the grave.

The verses of Sūrat al-Muṭaffifīn give the name of that place, for it says that the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyīn, and asks what will make a person realise what ʿIlliyyīn is, and answers that it is a written record witnessed by those brought near (83:18-21). And there is another verse of the Qur'an on the same subject, which says that good words are taken up to Allah, and that good deeds raise them.

The account of the disbeliever runs the other way. Angels come down with dark and terrifying faces, carrying a coarse ragged piece of cloth, and they sit in front of him. Then the angel of death draws his soul out the way a thorny branch is pulled out of wet wool wrapped around it, and the stench of that soul is worse than the stench of a dead animal gone bad. As the angels carry it up, other angels ask whose evil soul this is, and the answer gives the worst of the names he was known by. At the first heaven they ask for the gate to be opened, and it is not opened. The command comes that his record is to be kept in Sijjīn, which is where the record of the disobedient is kept. And his soul is thrown down.

The soul returns to the grave, and the angels who keep the account make him sit up and ask him the same questions the believer was asked. His answer to every one of them is nothing but that he does not know. His bed there is made of the Fire, and so is what he is dressed in, and a door is opened in his grave that faces the Fire, so that the heat and the flames reach him without stopping.

So the spirits of the deniers are carried all the way to the gate of the heaven, and there the door stays shut, and they are thrown back down. That is another way to take the words about the gates: they name the hour of death, and not the Day of Resurrection.

### Where these verses sit in the passage

A pledge was taken from every human being back in the world of spirits, before any of them was born into this world of bodies. What the pledge required was that when the prophets come with guidance and with instructions, a person should listen to them seriously and then do what he has heard. They were told that those who keep the pledge and carry out what it involves will be saved from every sorrow and will deserve lasting peace and comfort, and that those who deny the prophets or rebel against the instructions they bring will have the lasting punishment of Jahannam waiting for them.

The verses that follow present what actually happened once different groups of people came into the world and behaved differently. Some of them threw the pledge away behind their backs and set themselves against it, and others held to it and acted rightly. The end of the two groups, with their reward and their punishment, is set out in the four verses that run from verse 40 to verse 43. Verses 40 and 41 describe the deniers and the criminals, and verses 42 and 43 describe the believers and the mindful who fulfilled the pledge. So this verse is the opening of a two-part conclusion, and the word "wicked" at its close is answered by the word "wrongdoers" at the close of the next.

### Why the arrogance was there in the first place

The question goes deeper than the sentence. Why is it that when God's messengers give the call to the truth, the egotism of the people they address stops them from accepting it? The reason lies in what each side has to stand on. What the caller has is argument. What the person he is addressing has is material glory. The caller stands on the strength of what he can prove, and the other man stands on something he can see and touch. The force of an argument cannot be seen or touched.

That difference is what breeds the egotism. It makes a man judge the one who calls him to be lower in rank than himself, and it hands him what looks like a reason to ignore him. So that person's admission to the mercy of God is as hopeless as the camel at the needle's eye. They set God at nothing, and God sets them at nothing. God gave them glimpses of Himself through the one who called them, and He presented Himself to them in the form of arguments, and they treated none of it as important and refused to bow to it. How should people like that have any share in the bounty of God?

### In short

- The gates of heaven are closed to their deeds and to their souls, on the two readings, and a third reading combines the two.
- Paradise is as closed to them as the eye of a needle is to a camel, and the point of the image is that their punishment does not end.
- The report of the soul at death describes the gate that opens for the believer and the gate that stays shut for the disbeliever, with the record kept in ʿIlliyyīn for one and in Sijjīn for the other.
- The verse opens the conclusion of the passage, and the two verses about the deniers are answered by the two verses about the believers that follow.
- The arrogance of the address came from what each side had to stand on, since argument cannot be seen and material glory can.

41.text:
The second verse describes what is waiting inside. "Hell will be their bed; flames will be their cover. This is how We reward the wrongdoers". The verse gives them a bed and a covering, and both of them are made of the same thing.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Hell will be their bed"** translates a word that means a place of rest, a bed, or a floor. What is meant is that the bed they lie on comes from the Fire. This is how Muhammad bin Kaʿb al-Quraẓī explained it, and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk bin Muzāḥim and as-Suddī said the same.

**"flames will be their cover"** translates a plural word for something that covers, and the singular of it means a covering. The top sheet over them comes from the Fire as well. Another reading of it is simply that above them hangs a covering of torment.

**"This is how We reward the wrongdoers"** closes the verse, and the wrongdoers here are the idolaters, the people who went past the limits set for them and turned away from their Lord.

### Why the two verses close differently

The two verses end in almost the same way, and they are not quite the same. The verse before this one ends by naming the wicked, and this one ends by naming the wrongdoers. The difference is deliberate, and the reason given for it is that the second description is the more severe of the two. So the word moves from one fault to a heavier one as the punishment moves from being shut out to being shut in.

The picture itself is put in the plainest everyday idiom. A bed and a covering are the two things a person needs to rest. The verse takes both of them and makes both of them out of the Fire, so that rest itself becomes the punishment. For these people there is nothing to lie on and nothing to lie under that is not burning. It is the most eloquent way there is of saying, in ordinary words, that the punishment is extreme.

### In short

- The bed and the covering are both from the Fire, so that rest itself is taken away from them.
- The words for the bed and the covering are explained by al-Quraẓī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and as-Suddī.
- The verse closes on the wrongdoers where the one before it closed on the wicked, and the change of word marks the more severe of the two.
- The idiom is an ordinary one, and it is used to carry an extreme meaning.
